idees.affirmation: « On perd la plupart de sa chaleur par la tête. »

panneaux.titre: Par la tête, on perd au plus

panneaux.texte: Toute partie du corps laissée nue perd de la chaleur, pas seulement la tête.

sources.titre: Do We Really Lose Half our Body Heat From our Heads?
sources.extrait: At most, according to a 2008 report in BMJ, a person loses 7 percent to 10 percent of their body heat through their head.

sources.titre: Don't be fooled: six holiday health myths verified or debunked
sources.extrait: Some heat does escape through the head but certainly not the bulk of it, according to the researchers. […] Heat loss is proportional to the body's surface area that is exposed. Your head has a decent amount of surface area, […] but notes that the arms, legs and torso do, too.

sources.titre: Scientists Shed Light On Festive Medical Myths
sources.extrait: But recent studies have debunked this old soldier's tale. […] Any uncovered part of the body loses heat and will drop the core body temperature proportionately.

idees.affirmation: « Un bébé a plus d'os qu'un adulte. »

panneaux.voix: Environ 300 os à la naissance, et 206 chez l'adulte.

panneaux.texte: En grandissant, de petits os se soudent entre eux pour en former de plus grands.

sources.titre: How Many Bones Does a Baby Have?
sources.extrait: A newborn has 275 to 300 bones, while most adults have 206. […] As a baby grows, their smaller bones join together to create larger bones.
At birth, a baby's body has about 300 bones. These eventually fuse (grow together) to form the 206 bones that adults have.

sources.titre: You'll never have as many bones as you did at birth (and other strange skeleton facts)
sources.extrait: Newborns can have more than 300 distinct bones.

idees.affirmation: « Le plus petit os du corps se trouve dans l'oreille. »

panneaux.texte: C'est l'un des trois osselets de l'oreille, et le plus petit.
Il mesure de 2,6 à 3,4 mm de long.

sources.titre: What's the largest bone in the human body? (What about the smallest?)
sources.extrait: But no matter the age of an individual, the smallest bones in the human body are found in the ear. […] The smallest of the ossicles is the stapes. […] It measures about 0.1 to 0.13 inches (2.6 to 3.4 millimeters) in length.
It's the smallest bone in the human body, measuring only a few millimeters in both width and height.
measures 2.6-3.4 mm (0.1-0.13 in) in length and weighs from 2 to 4.3 mg (0.03- 0.066 grains).

idees.affirmation: « Les ongles et les cheveux continuent de pousser après la mort. »

panneaux.texte: Après la mort, le corps se déshydrate et la peau se rétracte.
panneaux.sous_texte: Elle découvre une partie des ongles et des cheveux.

panneaux.texte: Ongles et cheveux semblent plus longs… mais ils ne poussent plus.

sources.titre: Do Hair and Nails Keep Growing After Death?
sources.extrait: The short answer is no, though it may not seem that way to the casual observer. […] That's because after death, the human body dehydrates, causing the skin to shrink. […] This shrinking exposes the parts of the nails and hair that were once under the skin, causing them to appear longer

sources.titre: Do Hair and Nails Continue to Grow After Death?
sources.extrait: your hair and nails do not continue to grow after you die. […] Our flesh dries and, in so doing, pulls away from nails and hair.

sources.editeur: UAMS Health (Université de l'Arkansas pour les sciences médicales)
sources.titre: Do a person's hair and fingernails continue to grow after death?
sources.extrait: Hair and fingernails may appear longer after death, but not because they are still growing. […] After death, dehydration causes the skin and other soft tissues to shrink.
